articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont will feature Erwin Chemerinsky, Dean of Berkeley Law School in a discussion on Tuesday, March 1 at 4 p.m. He is a nationally recognized expert on the U.S. Supreme Court and election law. This event is part of the League’s 2022 Defending Democracy Speaker Series and is co-sponsored by local Leagues in Oakland, Santa Barbara, Solano County, Portland, OR; Gunnison Valley, CO; Pueblo, CO, Pike’s Peak Region, CO; and Collier County, FL. Chemerinsky became the 13th Dean of Berkeley Law School on July 1, 2017, when he joined the faculty as the Jesse H. Choper Distinguished Professor of Law. Prior to assuming this position he was the founding Dean and Distinguished Professor of Law, and Raymond Pryke Professor of First Amendment Law, at the University of California in Irvine. Before that, he was Professor of Law and Political Science at Duke University from 2004-2008, and from 1983-2004 was a professor at the University of Southern California Law School, teaching public interest Law, legal ethics, and political science. Chemerinsky is the author of 14 books, including leading casebooks and treatises about constitutional law, criminal procedure, and federal jurisdiction. His most recent books are Presumed Guilty: How the Supreme Court Empowered the Police and Subverted Civil Rights (Norton 2021), and The Religion Clauses: The Case for Separating Church and State (with Howard Gillman) (Oxford University Press 2020). Erwin Chemerinsky, Dean of Berkeley Law School. He also is the author of more than 200 law review articles. He is a contributing writer for the Opinion section of the Los Angeles Times and writes regular columns for the Sacramento Bee, the ABA Journal, and the Daily Journal, and frequent op-eds in newspapers across the country. He frequently argues appellate cases, including the U.S. Supreme Court. In 2016, he was named a fellow of the American Academy of Arts and Sciences. In 2017, National Jurist magazine again named Dean Chemerinsky as the most influential person in legal education in the United States. In January 2021, he was named President-elect of the Association of American Law Schools. This talk will be held live on Zoom and YouTube and will include an audience question and answer session. articles.text: Community Church has returned to in-person worship following a two-month hiatus due to the COVID Omicron surge in January. In-person worship at the church returned with live service at 10 a.m. this past Sunday, February 20. The service was led by Don Ashburn, with a sermon by Steve Schibsted. This is the first in-person worship since December 19, 2021. On October 2, 2021, Piedmont Community Church issued an announcement alerting residents of a COVID incident - church staff was informed that a volunteer who was in the Christian Education Building two days prior had tested positive for COVID-19. The person who was infected is fully vaccinated and was double-masked. Online-only worship was available through February 13. “The rapid emergence of the highly transmissible Omicron variant since December has created huge challenges for public health and community. Such a surge comes at a time when we all expected a return to at least a ‘new normal’ with effective vaccines,” said Joan Chow, a member of the Church’s Reopening Task Force. “But instead, we’ve had to make difficult decisions - such as cancelling in-person services from Christmas Eve services through [February 13] to protect the congregation as a whole.” The Reopening Task Force Members include Chow, Pastors Schibsted and Ashburn, Pat Leicher, Steve Senter, Randy Litteneker, Kristin Johnson, Toni Fischer, Leslie Quantz, Jay Foreman, and Tom Walter. The Church’s Reopening Task Force met in the winter months to assist in the planning for resuming in-person worship and advised the public through a emailed newsletter that “if cases and hospitalizations decline sufficiently, [the] proposed target date for in-person worship is February 20,” and that to resume in-person worship, masks would be required regardless of recent changes in County guidance. When attending an in-person service, proof of vaccination or a negative COVID-19 test obtained within 48 hours is required for entry. Masks indoors are required as well. If you do not have a mask, one will be provided to you. Piedmont Community Church

articles.text: The Piedmont Police Department provided its year-end 2021 crime report to City Council on Tuesday, February 22. The report found that there was a notable increase in larceny and theft incidents, but a decrease in burglaries. There were 280 reported offenses of larceny, or theft, in 2021, as opposed to 236 reported offenses the year prior. Larceny is described as theft that does not involve trespassing into a structure or vehicle. The major difference between larceny and burglary is the act of “breaking in.” Burglaries decreased from 61 reported incidents in 2020 to 25 reported incidents last year. “While the Police Department conducts proactive patrols to mitigate thefts and other crimes, we cannot overemphasize the importance of residents and visitors employing basic crime prevention actions such as not leaving valuables in vehicles,” Police Chief Jeremy Bowers explained in the Department’s report. There were no home-invasion style robberies in 2021, which Bowers described as a “testament to the outstanding initial response by patrol officers, investigative work by the Detective Unit, and the Department ability to leverage technology.” In the seven robberies that occurred last year, Piedmont Police identified and arrested suspects in four instances. Touting the efficiency of Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) cameras, the report included that officers made 30 arrests and recovered 34 stolen vehicles with a valuation of $449,500 with ALPR assistance; by comparison, 17 arrests and 34 vehicles were recovered in 2020, with a valuation of $167,300. The Department has used ALPR technology since 2013 and is in the process of implementing a Public Safety Camera program, approved by City Council last year. “The current phase of the implementation consists of working with the data fiber provider and utility company to bring the necessary infrastructure to the camera locations. The Department is very appreciative for the assistance of Public Works Director Daniel Gonzalez through this process,” Chief Bowers said. Total calls for service increased last year, from 9,844 in 2020 to 10,636 in 2021. The report found that there was a notable increase in larceny and theft incidents, but a decrease in burglaries. There were 280 reported offenses of larceny, or theft, in 2021, as opposed to 236 reported offenses the year prior. Larceny is described as theft that does not involve trespassing into a structure or vehicle. The major difference between larceny and burglary is the act of “breaking in.” Burglaries decreased from 61 reported incidents in 2020 to 25 reported incidents last year. “While the Police Department conducts proactive patrols to mitigate thefts and other crimes, we cannot overemphasize the importance of residents and visitors employing basic crime prevention actions such as not leaving valuables in vehicles,” Police Chief Jeremy Bowers explained in the Department’s report. There were no home-invasion style robberies in 2021, which Bowers described as a “testament to the outstanding initial response by patrol officers, investigative work by the Detective Unit, and the Department ability to leverage technology.” In the seven robberies that occurred last year, Piedmont Police identified and arrested suspects in four instances. Touting the efficiency of Automated License Plate Reader (ALPR) cameras, the report included that officers made 30 arrests and recovered 34 stolen vehicles with a valuation of $449,500 with ALPR assistance; by comparison, 17 arrests and 34 vehicles were recovered in 2020, with a valuation of $167,300. The Department has used ALPR technology since 2013 and is in the process of implementing a Public Safety Camera program, approved by City Council last year. “The current phase of the implementation consists of working with the data fiber provider and utility company to bring the necessary infrastructure to the camera locations. The Department is very appreciative for the assistance of Public Works Director Daniel Gonzalez through this process,” Chief Bowers said. Total calls for service increased last year, from 9,844 in 2020 to 10,636 in 2021. articles.text: Young People’s Symphony Orchestra (YPSO) will perform its winter concert at First Congregational Church of Berkeley this Saturday, February 26, at 8 p.m. Six musicians from Piedmont High School are members of YPSO: Violinists Jacob Hsia, Isabella Wu, and Cameryn Kwong; Eleanor Vo, (viola) Caitlin Gong (cello); and Samantha Cheunkarndee (violin). All are seniors except Cheunkarndee, a freshman. This year marks YPSO’s 85th season and 33rd season under the baton of Maestro David Ramadanoff. More than Over 90 young musicians, ranging in age from 12 to 19, will perform. The concert will include the works of Dmitiri Shostakovich, and two living American composers, Jennifer Higdon and Adolphus Hailstork. The first half of the program will feature Blue Cathedral by Higdon and Epitaph of a Man Who Dreamed by Hailstork. Higdon described her piece as “about deciding if life was going to be about living or about death.” In describing his work, Hailstork said “I believe that African Americans deserve to have the same homage paid to their suffering, and to their glories when they occur, as has happened throughout all of Western history.” The concert was rescheduled for Martin Luther King, Jr. Day, January 17, but was rescheduled due to COVID-19 concerns. Tickets can be purchased by visiting http://www.ypsomusic.org/tickets, or calling the box office at (510) 849-9776. The units are more energy efficient and work for both heating and cooling. “These are essentially heat pumps, that get rid of gas to become electric only. [This] sets us up to be a green, sustainable district, slowing moving away from gas and away from a carbon footprint,” explained Palmer. Dept. summer camp registrations begin March 1 By Allyson Aleksey The Piedmont Recreation Department will begin accepting signups by residents for its summer camps and programs starting Tuesday, March 1, at 9 a.m. Registration for non-residents begins on March 15. Summer programs this year include the popular and quickto-fill Camp Everything, which offers a variety of activities geared toward kids of all ages. Camp Everything’s full-day and half-day programs combine the interests of youth athletes, chefs, technologists, scientists, and artists. Many other summer programs will be offered for specific age groups, such as Discovery Camp; Outdoor Explorers; Camp 1973; Counselor in Training (CIT); and Summer Schoolmates. All programs offered by the Recreation Department will adhere to the most current state, county, and local COVID safety guidelines. Participants are required to complete a health screener prior to camp entry each day. Summer programs begin on June 6 and are as follows: • Week 1: June 6–10 • Week 2: June 13–17 • Week 3: June 20–24 • Week 4: June 27–July 17 • Week 5: July 5–8 • Week 6: July 11–15 • Week 7: July 18–22 • Week 8: July 25–29 • Week 9: August 1–5 To sign up when registration becomes available, and to view an activity guide for summer 2022, visit: https://www.ci.piedmont.ca.us/cms/One.aspx?portal Id=13659823&pageId=17506926. articles.text: The Piedmont Community Service Crew’s “5K Mask Project” is an opportunity for our local community to work together on a simple task that will increase the supply of N95 masks, so urgently needed by health care workers and the general public. Many cannot afford to buy these to protect everyone’s health. On the weekend of March 5th & 6th we plan to have dozens of volunteers working simultaneously outdoors refurbishing N95 masks. The work project will be held at the Dress Best for Less parking lot, 799 Magnolia Avenue, across the street from Piedmont High School. Volunteer hours Saturday, March 5, 12:30 to 4:30 p.m. Sunday, March 6, 10:00 a.m. to 3:30 p.m. This event is being hosted by the Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC), a co-ed Venturing Crew that empowers teens through service and leadership opportunities. PCSC is currently making a big push to get 5,000 refurbished masks completed as soon as we can – precisely why your help at this event is making such a direct impact in helping us reach our goals. This will be a lively event with snacks and music and will be a fun and rewarding way to help others and meet new people. The project is recommended for middle schoolers and older. Anyone younger should come with a parent. For additional information, contact PCSC Vice Presidents Valentina Prieto-Black at valentinaprietoblack@icloud.com or Elena Stevenson at elena.stev@ gmail.com, or Crew Advisor Ken Li at ken.i.li@sbcglobal.com.

articles.text: As we discussed last month, we often neglect the cognitive skills that are used and developed and only focus on the subject matter that is being taught and learned. However, it is often these cognitive skills that have a more lasting benefit to students. Knowing history to avoid repeating it and appreciating literature is valuable. But what are the skills involved in liberal arts classes? The ability to understand another person’s ideas and perspective from their writing is one important skill. There are certainly others, but since this can be so tricky, we’ll just stick to that for today. What are They Trying to Tell Me? I remember I was reading Tom Sawyer in middle school and was going to write an essay on it. My brother was helping me and asked, “Why do you think Mark Twain wrote this book?” “To entertain people?” I asked. “Well partly that’s true,” he told me. “But there is almost always a deeper message about the world.” That message stuck with me and helped me navigate my English and Liberal Arts classes and reading in general for the rest of my life. Where Are They Coming From? Once you have figured out what an author is trying to tell you there is an important second step that we can take: how does this person see the world? This ability to see someone else’s perspective Students gain perspective through reading. is invaluable in navigating our complex and diverse world. Understanding Isn’t Empathy Too often the concept of “understanding” has a connotation of feeling for someone or not hating them. And sometimes this is true. Understanding someone’s point of view can help you see things differently and maybe your anger might dissipate. But feeling for them is not the goal and we can’t avoid seeing someone’s perspective because we don’t believe their perspective deserves our attention. You can never defeat your enemy if you don’t know where he is hiding. Why bother trying to understand how a KKK member sees the world? So that you can turn them or defeat them, not necessarily because I want to heal them. Reading for Perspective Reading to understand someone else’s point of view is not something that comes naturally. When reading it, it requires looking specifically at things that don’t make sense or seem wrong and figuring out what they must be thinking to see things this way. “What the heck are they thinking?!” needs to become a question, not an insult. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2022. articles.text: The Piedmont Cub Scout Day Camp, which takes place in Dracena Park the first week that school is out for the summer, is coming up fast. This year Piedmont Cubs and all youth (1st to 5th graders) will be traveling back in time with the theme: Wild, Wild West. With the help of an outstanding camp staff, the Piedmont Scout Council is excited to be offering a wide range of activities, most especially the archery range. Other activities will include Scout skills, games, songs and crafts. The Piedmont Fire Department will highlight the week with the traditional Egg Drop on the last day of camp as parents and families enjoy a picnic while watching the Egg Drop. Returning leadership includes 2021 Camp President Mollie King, Camp Crew Advisor Ken Li and Camp Director Keri Ichimaru. Eagle Scout Jack Gros is new to the team, bringing fresh ideas and energy. Along with other staff and leaders, they’re putting together an ace-high program for the adventures in Dracena Park. “I am always on the lookout for youth who respond positively to opportunities to take charge of what their crew is planning.” said Li. “During the past three years… our annual Cub Scout Day Camp [has] been entirely planned and run by teens.” “It was great to see how well the staff interacted with the younger Cubs,” noted Ichimaru about the 2021 camp. “Day Camp is a highlight of the program year,” confirmed Scout Executive Kate Benson. “Youth get a chance to be outside, bellow through songs, make new friends, and enjoy a week of fun. It’s something we look forward to all year.” Interested youth can register for camp through the Piedmont Recreation Department (piedmont.ca.gov/activityguide). Registration opens on March 1st for Piedmont residents and March 15th for non-residents. Youth interested in joining Cub Scouts, Scouts BSA, Venturing Units, or Exploring are encouraged to contact the Piedmont Scout Council for more information at 510-547-4493 or contact@piedmontbsa.org. For more information, visit the webpage at www.piedmontbsa.org, or mosey down and visit the Scouting staff at the office at 10 Highland Way in Piedmont. articles.text: Theatre is back! Yes, across the Bay Area, we are starting to see signs of life returning to our stages. For many companies, it has been over 600 days since we last turned on our stage lights, donned costumes, dusted off the props and welcomed audiences in a traditional way. Yes, we have streamed, zoomed, performed outdoors, created audio plays and musicals and so many other ways that the theatre world has put our innovation to the test, but in the end, we have all missed the specific and unique energy between performers and an audience. Theatre gives us a window into our own hearts and reminds us of the stories of others. Our empathy and imagination muscles are ready to be flexed! For our young people, attending theatre can inspire kids to see beyond the boundaries of their world and dream big, while also stimulating the parts of their creative spirits that are yearning to express themselves. As Bay Area Children’s Theatre returns we are focussing on this aspect of imagination like never before. We have been on a slightly more delayed timeline as some of the adult companies to ensure that at least our 5 and up audience members have the opportunity to be vaccinated. Our new musical, The Imaginaries: An Immersive Musical, opening March 19th in Berkeley, transports the audience to the Imaginary World, where imaginary friends live and train for their work with humans. This production is based on the book “Pocket Guide for Imaginary Friends”, which was written by our writing team and is now available on amazon.com and Photo by Melissa Nigro. A family enjoys a Bay Area Children’s Theater performance. through the BACT website. The book and the show celebrate imagination and creativity as a means to dream up amazing adventures. As we return to the theatre, for both adults and kids, I look forward to the incredible power of storytelling to help us shape a brighter future. The conversations in the car in the ride home, the artistic expression that are inspired by a show, the connection that happens within an audience–these are all means of expressing ourselves, communicating with others and connecting with the world around us! Let the curtain rise and welcome in a new moment of inspiration and innovation. Nina Meehan is Executive Direct of Bay Area Children’s Theatre. “The Imaginaries: An Immersive Musical,” open March 19 at the Osher Studio in downtown Berkeley, 2055 Center Street. Tickets available: https:// bactheatre.org/tickets-events/ the-imaginaries/

articles.text: Piedmont powers past St. Mary’s 76-50, Swett 74-14 Piedmont’s No. 2 seeded girls’ basketball team is set to square off with No. 3 Lick-Wilmerding tonight, Wednesday, February 23 at 7:00 p.m. in the North Coast Section semifinals at Binks Rawlings Gym. The girls powered their way past No. 10 St. Mary’s 76-50 on Saturday, February 19 in the quarterfinals, and demolished No. 15 Swett 74-14 in the opening round on Wednesday, February 16. Should PHS be victorious tonight, they advance to their first NCS finals appearance since 2011. The team has already qualified for the CIF State Tournament. Winning the NCS title would give them a higher seed in the state playoffs. “We’ve been wanting to start strong and compete right from the jump, and the girls have done a really good job of that,” said coach Bryan Gardere. “We’re very excited to be this far. Sophomore guard Natalia Martinez picked up the slack with 33 points. “Trinity came out early and I knew what I had to do and what we had to do as a team,” said Martinez. “We can’t always depend on her to score and get rebounds, so we had to step up.” Zamora is fine and returned to practice the next day. articles.text: Highlanders open season with 8-1 win vs San Ramon Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team opened its 2022 spring season with a dominating 8-1 victory over San Ramon Valley at the Wolves’ home courts on Thursday, February 17. Last season, the North Coast Section did not offer an individual or team tournament due to the Covid-related shortened schedule. “I don’t think there is anyone that can challenge us in the league (WACC), said PHS coach Jim, Landes, “but with NCS, we’ll see how University. HeadRoyce seems to have a strong team, too. We have both of them on the schedule, so that will be a good measuring point for us.” Piedmont enters its season with a wealth of returning talent and some new, gifted players. Senior Charlie Lambert is a fouryear starter, while classmates Charlie Olcott and Kai Baudendistel are third-year lettermen. Seniors Charlie Sullivan, Graham McWeeny, Oliver Maxwell, and Carson Hicks are entering their second year on varsity. “We have a lot of quality depth and experience, which is good to have. Kai and Charlie [Olcott] will likely start off as No. 1 doubles again, but I know they’d like to be in the singles lineup. There’s going to be some competition,” said Landes. Sophomore Monte Imburg is back after earning the Post’s Freshman of the Year award last year. Imburg is earning a spot as a singles starter after mostly appearing at doubles last season. Sophomore Ben Breber will return. “Monte is No. 3 right now and he and Ben will compete for that third spot. It’ll be close, Monte has gotten better,” said Landes. Bursting onto the scene as a junior is Lenni Burchardt, an exchange student from Germany. He is likely to play No. 2 singles. “Our No. 2 is very good. He’s an exchange student and is just here for this year. He may end up getting some time at No. 1. He and Charlie [Lambert] are going to push each other,” said Landes. Ethan Pham is a junior and a second-year starter who Landes thinks will make an impact. Landes also had high praise for firstyear varsity players senior Jacob Hsia, sophomore Graham Alban and freshman Nick King. “Ethan Pham is another guy competing to be in the singles lineup. Right now we’re playing Staff Photos Charlie Lambert is a four-year starter and plays at No. 1 singles. six singles matches but we may see him at doubles when we have to play four singles and three doubles. He played really well last season with Oliver Maxwell at doubles,” said Landes. The Highlanders have a busy week ahead at the start of March. They host Campolindo on March 1, play College Prep on March 2, Encinal on March 3, then head to Fresno for the California Tennis Classic on March 4-5. Piedmont will compete in Division 1 at the tournament after winning the Division 2 ladder in 2020 prior to the pandemic. San Ramon Valley results Piedmont’s 8-1 victory at San Ramon included claiming winning five of six singles matches and all three doubles matches. Lambert won No. 1 singles in two very close sets 7-6 (6-4), 6-4. Burchardt appeared at No. 2 and won handily 6-1, 6-0. At No. 3, Imburg also won 6-1, 6-0. Pham appeared at No. 4 singles and won 6-1, 6-4. At No. 5 Olcott breezed to a 6-3, 6-0 victory. At No. 6, Baudendistel battled in a close three-set loss, 4-6, 6-3, 10-6. In doubles, Sullivan and McWeeny paired to win at No, 1 in three sets, 5-7, 7-6 (6-4), 10-4. Maxwell and King won at No. 2 doubles, 6-4, 6-4, and Hsia and Graham Alban won 6-1, 6-4 at No. 3 doubles. NEXT UP Piedmont (1-0) hosts Campolindo on Tuesday, March 1 at 3:30 p.m. at the Corey Reich Tennis Center, then plays College Prep the next day, also at the same time. PHS heads to Encinal in Alameda on Thursday, March 3, then travels to Fresno on Friday for the two-day California Tennis Classic. Charlie Olcott (front) and Kai Baudendistel make a strong senior doubles team.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont has launched an online survey for residents to provide input on the Piedmont Community Pool programming. The pool is set to open in summer 2024; the final design phase was recently approved by City Council. The 15-minute survey is geared toward aquatic programming and focuses on the community’s interest in various programming opportunities at the new aquatic facility. The Piedmont Recreation Department compiled a wide variety of programming to start understanding the community’s interests. Guaranteed programming is listed first, followed by additional options that residents may “rank.” Guaranteed programming includes the yearround Piedmont Swim Team, high school water polo and swim teams, lap swimming, swim lessons, open swim, and lifeguard training. At the completion of the survey, an overall site plan from community workshops is available so that residents may view and provide additional comments or suggestions. To complete the survey, visit https://www.surveymonkey. com/r/Piedmontcommunitypoolprogramming.

articles.text: A retrospective of geometric art by the late Bill Blackwell will be on display at the Piedmont Center for the Arts from noon to 2 p.m. on Sunday, February 27. An architect by profession with a lifelong love of geometry, Blackwell’s art work consists of large collages of geometric shapes painted in bright colors, mounted on Masonite. He was fascinated by the possibilities of combining basic shapes and colors into dynamic art. Before he passed away in November 2021, Blackwell also was working on a book he tentatively titled Explorations in Geometry, which focuses on the mathematical beauty of plain geometry and its multiple uses in the built environment. In the book’s introduction, Blackwell noted, “Galileo was one of the first modern thinkers to clearly state that the laws of nature are mathematical. In The Assayer, published in 1623, Galileo wrote ‘philosophy is written in this grand book, the universe… It is written in the language of mathematics, and its characters are triangles, circles, and other geometric figures.’” Blackwell’s first book, Geometry in Architecture, was published by John Wiley & Sons in 1983. His art was previously exhibited at Piedmont Center for the Arts the day it opened in August 2011. His vivid yellow geometric design was the principal work of art and located above the stage. He earlier had a large art exhibit at the former Metro Center in downtown Oakland. He also exhibited his art at the Mathematical Science Research Institute at UC Berkeley, the Hearst Gallery at St. Mary’s College in Moraga, and a gallery in Pt. Reyes. Blackwell received his undergraduate degree at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and his master’s degree in architecture at UC Berkeley. During his career, he was employed by the architecture firm Skidmore and Merrill, the San Francisco Redevelopment Agency, and the Bechtel Corporation for 20 years. He is survived by his wife Marjorie of Piedmont. This work of geometric art by Bill Blackwell was first shown in Piedmont on opening day of the Piedmont Center for the Arts in 2011. articles.text: Writer and artist Chanel Miller’s exhibit, entitled I was, I am, I will be, is being shown on the exterior wall of the San Francisco Asian Art Museum on Hyde Street and is free for everyone to view. Miller was first known publicly as Emily Doe, the victim of sexual assault by a student at Stanford University in 2015. The victim impact statement she wrote and read at her assailant’s sentencing hearing the following year went viral and was read 11 million times within four days. The case gained international recognition because the assailant, a 19-year-old male athlete, received a sentence of three months in jail. The case influenced the California legislature to require prison terms for rapists whose victims were unconscious. Judge Persky, who handed down the light sentence, was recalled from office by county voters in 2018. Miller’s memoir detailing the tragic event caught the attention of the Asian Art Museum’s head of Contemporary Art, Abby Chen. “Not only is she an amazChanel Miller’s exhibit I was, I am, I will be seen from the exterior of the Asian museum. ing writer, she’s also this visual artist...she’s incredibly young,” Chen said. Chen and museum staff began the process of collaborating with Miller. Growing up in Palo Alto, Miller said she frequented the museum, but never dreamed she would be featured one day. “Whenever I was upset, I’d take a sharpie to the wall and sit for hours and let these ‘creatures’ come to life. I could create landscapes that don’t have narrow borders. That’s the scene that came out of this feeling,” Miller said. Even though the museum’s doors were closed due to the COVID pandemic, Miller’s exhibit was visible without visitors setting foot in the building. At night, Miller’s black and white figures are illuminated and visible from the street. “The whole journey of healing is never linear,” Miller said, adding that she hopes the piece will be seen as universal and not confined to her particular experience.

Don Quixote, based on the classic novel by Miguel de Cervantes, is filled with physical humor and fiery dancing - Artistic Director and Principal Choreographer Helgi Tomasson said one of the production’s most appealing aspects is “the joy it gives you - you could say it’s a bit of a farce, nothing dramatic or psychological. It’s upbeat and fun.” Don Quixote first took the stage at San Francisco Ballet in 2003, and over the years has been updated by Tomasson. In 2012, award-winning costume designer Martin Pakledinaz introduced 19th-century Spanish garb and visually striking scenery. In reworking the classic story, Paklendinaz, who passed away shortly after the 2012 premiere, said “it’s important to drop what you’ve seen and try to make it your original production.” Performances will be at 8 p.m. in the War Memorial Opera House on Saturday, February 26 at 8 p.m., Sunday, February 27 at 2 p.m., and daily through March 6. articles.text: Artist Robert Brokl will have an exhibit, “What I’ve Been Up To” at Piedmont Center for the Arts March 5–20. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays, with an artist’s reception on Sunday, March 13 at 2 p.m. The landscape-themed exhibition features recent paintings (oil and gouache), pastel drawings, and woodblock prints, with Brokl’s reflections of trips to the Southern Sierra Nevadas, the deserts of Death Valley and Anza Borrego, and the Mendocino area of California’s North Coast. It is a visual diary of recent travels, from the austere, spare deserts and the flora and fauna that survive temperature extremes. “What’s also become sadly apparent is how vulnerable these places are to the effects of the changing climate,” Brokl said. “My depictions of vast forests, azure lakes, and minimalist, unspoiled, primordial deserts are ‘Befores,’ and serve as records of these areas from before the 2020 Creek Fire.”

articles.text: Review by Jay Russell Wow. Watching The Matrix: Resurrections left me in a state of incoherence. Where do I start with the fourth iteration of the groundbreaking 1995 philosophical sci-fi thriller The Matrix? The original film, starring Keanu Reeves, Laurence Fishburne, and Carrie-Anne Moss, blew my mind at age 12 when I saw it at Jack London Theater. I was drawn into the theater this time expecting to find out what would happen if Neo (Keanu Reeves) took the blue pill and decided to stay in his “illusionary world” instead of taking the red pill, as he did in the original film for the inconvenient truth of the “real”, post-apocalyptic world. After watching the latest version, viewers should be warned that the word plot is a misnomer. The direction of the film felt like a lottery ball drawing, each scene more random with new irrelevant characters assuming desperate roles. It is two and half hours of irrelevance The original movie asked questions such as: What if the things you see are not real? What if you were chained up in a cave and all you knew were shadows on the wall, but never the things making the shadows. The first Matrix film is an allegory to a scenario called Plato’s Cave. The timeless philosophical situation was retold in the first Matrix with modern implications pertinent to religion, the limits of perception and the question of existence. In the new film Reeves plays Mr. Anderson, who did not evolve into the hero named Neo. Anderson is a techie in San Francisco, that designed a video game essentially bringing the world of “the Matrix” to life through video games. He is supposed to feel yearning for Carrie Anne Moss’s character “Trinity,” who lives in an unhappy marriage in this alternate scenario. But there is no chemistry; there are no sparks when they see each other at a coffee shop. The plot failed. Further, why was it filmed in San Francisco throughout the thick of the pandemic? It was pretty much created with computer graphics. I would compare it with the stinker Starship Troopers 2, which used b-roll stock footage from the original 1997 Starship Troopers in the sequel, pawning them off as new scenes. In the Matrix: Resurrections there were many flashbacks to the same footage from the first film. They were mixed in with rehashed scenes that felt like cover band performances. Any original content made little sense. A big mistake was the absence of the great actor Laurence Fishburne as Morpheus. Instead of just letting him be dead from the earlier film, he was “replaced” by two characters, a look-alike and some odd entity, possibly the digital version of Morpheus’ soul? Yikes, just let dead dogs lie. This film cost nearly one fifth of a billion dollars, a whopping $190 million, but earned $157 million at the box office. Perhaps they were lucky to lose only $33 million. Keanu Reeves looks ahead to a fourth movie in the John Wick series, which actually has Laurence Fishburne. Basically the John Wick films take all the awesome gunmanship and action from The Matrix and use a simple but effective plot: a retired hitman’s dog gets killed so he goes on a revenge killing spree. Where The Matrix series crumbles, John Wick succeeds. How many know that Keanu Reeves is actually a competitive marksman? He makes the action scenes in John Wick look real, because he knows what he is doing. But the new Matrix movie hardly ever put a gun in Reeves’ hand. That is like casting George Clooney in a Batman suit and mask so no one could see him. Is The Matrix: Resurrections worse than Batman and Robin (1997) with Clooney? Maybe not. Clooney himself said, “I think we may have killed [The Batman] franchise.” It’s a coin toss which was worse. The Matrix: Resurrections. Directed by Lana Wachowski. Starring Keanu Reeves, and Carrie Anne-Moss. 2 hrs., 28 min. Rated R. articles.text: Perhaps it’s time to banish that all too familiar line, “This is a chick flick,” no matter that the genre is still alive and well in Hollywood: young female twenty-somethings in the hunt for that special guy who will complete them. Yet there are also films about women who live very different lives and have very different definitions of what completes them. Case in point would be the recently released “It’s Complicated.” This is a woman’s movie to be sure; however, the target demographic is women 40 and older. Nancy Meyer (“Baby Boom,” “Something’s Gotta Give,” “The Holiday”) has been writing and directing romantic comedies about mature women for the better part of two decades. Her protagonists have had enough life experience to make insightful comparisons (that was then, this is now), bridling when things begin to feel hauntingly familiar. “It’s Complicated” has at its center the incomparable Meryl Streep, portraying Jane Adler, divorced for over a decade from Jake, played by Alec Baldwin. As a middle-aged woman, Jane has it all (well, almost all): a gorgeous, semi-rural home in Santa Barbara; a prosperous, up-scale bakery and café; three grown children; and is an accomplished chef. But still no man in her life. And therein is the rub. At her son’s NYU graduation (the whole family gathers in Manhattan), she unexpectedly has drinks and dinner with Jake with much dancing before and after. Jake is attending the ceremony without his younger wife, Agness (Lake Bell) – buff and demanding and the mother of 5-year-old Pedro. Drunk, swept away by familiar emotions and alcohol, they fall into bed and into an affair resurrecting all kinds of issues that had long ago been if not resolved at least buried. Jane is suddenly the other woman and completely unhinged by events. Jake is energized, captivated and even jealous of Jane’s casual flirtations with her architect, Adam (Steve Martin). The situation makes for engaging comedy. What Meyers does, and does well, is focus on a certain type of woman: mature, professional, once wounded, affluent and feeling she has been sleeping alone for far too long. Jane’s circle of friends, all contemporaries, equally attractive, are at first shocked when told about Jake; yet they remain supportive. Meyer is adept at creating a world that is more fantasy than reality, possessing a bright patina, a bit Disneyesque, lacking any semblance of grit, inspired, it seems, by Crate and Barrel, Architectural Digest and J. Crew. In a nice way. Meyer can easily be forgiven, however, for her movies always possess characters that are exceedingly charming and likable and the world Jane inhabits is deliciously seductive, bathed in a golden glow that brightens every moment. Of course Streep is brilliant, as always. She can actually elicit a laugh from the audience by a single, nuanced expression and she runs the gamut of emotions in the film with consummate ease. Her range and ability as an actress are astonishing. Take note of this year’s Julie and Julia, a role that will certainly result in a nomination. Alec Baldwin is also superb, playing the role of the chunky, aging, well-heeled, roguish husband, suddenly filled with a newly awakened lust and an abiding regret for what he left behind (children, hearth and wife of 20 years) when he wandered off and into the arms of Agness where gravity and age have yet to appear. Both Streep and Baldwin possess excellent comedic timing and make evident their deep well of talent in scene after scene. Though Baldwin is a strong presence in “It’s Complicated,” this is a woman’s film from the first frame and peruses women’s anxieties and issues with a pastiche of honesty and comedy. Meyers also appreciates a tidy ending and manages to find one that seems just right. It’s Complicated. Starring Meryl Streep, Alec Baldwin, Steve Martin, John Krasinski and Rita Wilson.Written and directed by Nancy Meyer. Rated R

GOOD THROUGH MARCH 2022 GOOD THROUGH MARCH 2022 GOOD THROUGH MARCH 2022 GOOD THROUGH MARCH 2022 It’s Complicated By Chris Honoré Perhaps it’s time to banish that all too familiar line, “This is a chick flick,” no matter that the genre is still alive and well in Hollywood: young female twenty-somethings in the hunt for that special guy who will complete them. Yet there are also films about women who live very different lives and have very different definitions of what completes them. Case in point would be the recently released “It’s Complicated.” This is a woman’s movie to be sure; however, the target demographic is women 40 and older. Nancy Meyer (“Baby Boom,” “Something’s Gotta Give,” “The Holiday”) has been writing and directing romantic comedies about mature women for the better part of two decades. Her protagonists have had enough life experience to make insightful comparisons (that was then, this is now), bridling when things begin to feel hauntingly familiar. “It’s Complicated” has at its center the incomparable Meryl Streep, portraying Jane Adler, divorced for over a decade from Jake, played by Alec Baldwin. As a middle-aged woman, Jane has it all (well, almost all): a gorgeous, semi-rural home in Santa Barbara; a prosperous, up-scale bakery and café; three grown children; and is an accomplished chef. But still no man in her life. And therein is the rub. At her son’s NYU graduation (the whole family gathers in Manhattan), she unexpectedly has drinks and dinner with Jake with much dancing before and after. Jake is attending the ceremony without his younger wife, Agness (Lake Bell) – buff and demanding and the mother of 5-year-old Pedro. Drunk, swept away by familiar emotions and alcohol, they fall into bed and into an affair resurrecting all kinds of issues that had long ago been if not resolved at least buried. Jane is suddenly the other woman and completely unhinged by events. Jake is energized, captivated and even jealous of Jane’s casual flirtations with her architect, Adam (Steve Martin). The situation makes for engaging comedy. What Meyers does, and does well, is focus on a certain type of woman: mature, professional, once wounded, affluent and feeling she has been sleeping alone for far too long. Jane’s circle of friends, all contemporaries, equally attractive, are at first shocked when told about Jake; yet they remain supportive. Meyer is adept at creating a world that is more fantasy than reality, possessing a bright patina, a bit Disneyesque, lacking any semblance of grit, inspired, it seems, by Crate and Barrel, Architectural Digest and J. Crew. In a nice way. Meyer can easily be forgiven, however, for her movies always possess characters that are exceedingly charming and likable and the world Jane inhabits is deliciously seductive, bathed in a golden glow that brightens every moment. Of course Streep is brilliant, as always. She can actually elicit a laugh from the audience by a single, nuanced expression and she runs the gamut of emotions in the film with consummate ease. Her range and ability as an actress are astonishing. Take note of this year’s Julie and Julia, a role that will certainly result in a nomination. Alec Baldwin is also superb, playing the role of the chunky, aging, well-heeled, roguish husband, suddenly filled with a newly awakened lust and an abiding regret for what he left behind (children, hearth and wife of 20 years) when he wandered off and into the arms of Agness where gravity and age have yet to appear. Both Streep and Baldwin possess excellent comedic timing and make evident their deep well of talent in scene after scene. Though Baldwin is a strong presence in “It’s Complicated,” this is a woman’s film from the first frame and peruses women’s anxieties and issues with a pastiche of honesty and comedy. Meyers also appreciates a tidy ending and manages to find one that seems just right. It’s Complicated. articles.text: Kodi Smit-McPhee and Benedict Cumberbatch in The Power of the Dog. Review by Chris Honoré The mythology of the American west is replete with images of men who are symbols of leathery masculinity and independence, two examples, among many, being John Wayne (The Searchers), and Clint Eastwood (Pale Rider). Now comes The Power of the Dog, released in the latter part of 2021, first in theaters and shortly thereafter on Netflix. It has received 12 Oscar nominations, one for Best Picture, and written and directed by Jane Campion. It is based on Thomas Savage’s 1967 novel of the same name. The film is set on a large cattle ranch in the wide expanses of Montana (the picture was actually shot in New Zealand). The year is 1925. The film stars Benedict Cumberbatch as Phil Burbank, Jesse Plemons as his brother George (they co-own the ranch), Kristen Dunst as the widowed Rose, and Kodi Smit-McPhee portraying Rose’s younger brother, Peter, a medical student. Phil is your classic, deliberately unwashed, and unrepentantly blunt rancher who calls George, always well-groomed, even when riding, “fatso.” He also takes cruel exception to Rose’s younger, somewhat effeminate brother Peter, who waits tables at Rose’s small town café, wears white canvas shoes instead of boots, and poses a startling contrast to the ranch’s cowhands – and to Phil’s departed mentor and role model, the quintessential cowboy known as Bronco Henry. He was a man who was the very definition of masculinity, no matter how toxic. As it turns out, George becomes enamored with Rose, and soon returns to the ranch with her as his new bride. For Phil, Rose’s very presence on the ranch fills him with resentment, seemingly for no other reason than she is a woman, and he takes a cruel pleasure in tormenting her. Soon the family (Peter has returned to the ranch from school for the summer) slips into dysfunction, and Rose begins to use alcohol to cope. Phil, of course, continues to play the role of rugged rancher, despite the fact that he graduated Phi Beta Kappa. from Yale University. Surprisingly, he decides to take Peter in hand, hoping to mold him in his own ersatz image. Strangely, Peter simultaneously resists and complies and a bond is unexpectedly created between the two that is complex, suggesting that there is almost a quasi-erotic aspect to their relationship. All of the above begs the question: did I find Power of the Dog compelling? Despite all of the praise the film has received, I found its plot elusive, its tone dark, its characters remote (the deconstruction by Campion of the American cowboy?), even puzzling. Phil, meanwhile, seems damaged beyond understanding, his bullying rage causing me to wonder if he is keeping a secret that to him is unthinkable, and the end of the film borders on the strange. Power of the Dog. Written and directed by Jane Campion. Starring Benedict Cumberbatch, Kristen Dunst, Jesse Plemons. Streaming on Netflix and in theaters. 2 hrs., 8 min. Rated R

articles.text: Small Foot, an animated feature released in 2018, is the name that Yetis, a massive furry creature, has given to humans. The Yeti live in a village, isolated on top of a mountain above the clouds in the Himalayas. The story opens with Yeti Migo (Channing Tatum), who is careful to live by the ancient laws of the stones, which are kept by the Stonekeeper (Common), the village leader. Migo is tasked with the job of hitting a gong each morning with his head, which the Yetis believe causes the sun to rise. One morning, distracted by Meechee, a cute Yeti, and the Stonekeeper’s daughter, upon whom he has a crush, Migo misses the gong and to his surprise lands outside the village where he witnesses a plane crash, piloted by a Small Foot, a human that the Yetis believe is mythical. Astonished, Migo races back to the village to tell everyone what he saw. The villagers refuse to believe Migo and banish him from the village. And thus begins Migo’s adventure, which includes spending time below the clouds, a place he never thought existed. It’s there that he meets a human named Percy (James Cordon), a wildlife documentarian, who has heard the tale of the existence of Migo from the pilot and is eager to film him as proof that such enormous creatures do exist. Percy’s situation is that he has lost his audience and sees filming Migo as a way of regaining his viewers. When Percy does meet Migo, he is initially scared, and in his panic he shoots himself with a tranquilizer gun. Migo puts the unconscious Percy in a sleeping bag and prepares to take him home to his village as proof that he was indeed telling the truth about the existence of the Small Foot. But on the way, above the clouds, the two are hit with a blizzard that freezes Percy solid. Migo tries to thaw Percy over a fire, something that terrifies the human who thinks Migo is preparing to eat him. Percy finally realizes that Migo has saved him, and they keep going, finally arriving at the Yeti’s mountaintop village. Of course, things get complicated and the villagers, especially Meechee, worry that Percy will reveal the location of their secret village and humans will find them. And there’s the difficulty that Percy and Migo and Meechee have communicating with this Small Foot. But finally they manage to find a way which allows them to resolve the misunderstandings that have existed between the Yetis and, well, the Small Feet. Small Foot. Animation. Directed by Karey Kirkpatrick. With voices of Channing Tatum, James Corden, and Zendaya. 1 hr. 36 min. Streaming by Warner Bros.

It was another beautiful morning and strong turnout for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group on February 16. There were 33 walkers, including Cheryl Papin, a friend of Susan Brown visiting from St. Louis. The warm weather has made for an early spring in terms of trees and flowers blooming early. Longtime locals have noted plants that once bloomed in March are now flowering in February, January, or even late December. Climate change seems to be the reason and is an existential problem. Daffodils made an appearance around town a week or two ago, and “tulip tree” magnolias were in bloom too. White and pink flowering fruit tree blossoms were just starting to pop and a joy to see. Over the weekend it was noted that on Huntleigh Road, just off Hampton Road there was a long line of trees with snow white blossoms on both sides of the street, and that they climbed all the way up its hill. Going to see this once-a-year spectacle seemed like a wonderful destination, so Huntleigh was the group’s destination for the day. The walkers went up Highland Avenue, crossing it to Sheridan Avenue, and down to its intersection with Wildwood Avenue. The home of Jacqueline Davis on this corner has lovely flowers in its garden throughout the year, so the group stopped and enjoyed them before taking the usual shortcut through the Hall Fenway. Crossing the street, the group walked through Crocker Park and enjoyed the large tulip magnolias on its north side; as well as the Benny Bufano statue of a mother bear with nursing cubs in the center of the park. The walkers passed the huge eucalyptus trees on Hampton Road where St. James Drive ends. The group continued on Hampton past Hampton Park, and pressed on up Hampton to Huntleigh. Going through the large, white columns originally marked the main entrance to the St. James Woods real estate development, they admired azaleas and in a beautifully landscaped front yard. Further up Hampton the walkers arrived at Huntleigh Road and caught their first sight of the white, flowering trees lining the street as far as they could see. As they continue up Huntleigh, they were surprised and delighted to see Carol Long. one of the group’s original members. She lives nearby told the group that the City planted flowering plum trees many years ago. The blossoming trees continued on Lexford, and the group followed them down its hill. Further down Lexford, just before Hampton, the walkers came to a unique, brick home built in a storybook architecture style with a brick block maze in the front yard. There is also a circular brick chimney and a wavy brick wall, as well as a terracotta tile roof. Architect Jim Kellogg, a regular Wednesday walker and a former member of the Piedmont Planning Commission pointed out that the house also has a unique brick garage to the right, and that there is a swimming pool in the back. It was then time to retrace their steps and head back to the Exedra. It had been a 3-1/2 mile walk in a little more than 90 minutes with natural beauty that can only be enjoyed this time of year. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday, rain or shine, at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. By Dick Carter It was another beautiful morning and strong turnout for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group on February 16. There were 33 walkers, including Cheryl Papin, a friend of Susan Brown visiting from St. Louis. The warm weather has made for an early spring in terms of trees and flowers blooming early. Longtime locals have noted plants that once bloomed in March are now flowering in February, January, or even late December. Climate change seems to be the reason and is an existential problem. Daffodils made an appearance around town a week or two ago, and “tulip tree” magnolias were in bloom too. White and pink flowering fruit tree blossoms were just starting to pop and a joy to see. Over the weekend it was noted that on Huntleigh Road, just off Hampton Road there was a long line of trees with snow white blossoms on both sides of the street, and that they climbed all the way up its hill. Going to see this once-a-year spectacle seemed like a wonderful destination, so Huntleigh was the group’s destination for the day. The walkers went up Highland Avenue, crossing it to Sheridan Avenue, and down to its intersection with Wildwood Avenue. The home of Jacqueline Davis on this corner has lovely flowers in its garden throughout the year, so the group stopped and enjoyed them before taking the usual shortcut through the Hall Fenway. Crossing the street, the group walked through Crocker Park and enjoyed the large tulip magnolias on its north side; as well as the Benny Bufano statue of a mother bear with nursing cubs in the center of the park. The walkers passed the huge eucalyptus trees on Hampton Road where St. James Drive ends. The group continued on Hampton past Hampton Park, and pressed on up Hampton to Huntleigh. Going through the large, white columns originally marked the main entrance to the St. James Woods real estate development, they admired azaleas and in a beautifully landscaped front yard. Further up Hampton the walkers arrived at Huntleigh Road and caught their first sight of the white, flowering trees lining the street as far as they could see. As they continue up Huntleigh, they were surprised and delighted to see Carol Long. one of the group’s original members. She lives nearby told the group that the City planted flowering plum trees many years ago. The blossoming trees continued on Lexford, and the group followed them down its hill. Further down Lexford, just before Hampton, the walkers came to a unique, brick home built in a storybook architecture style with a brick block maze in the front yard. There is also a circular brick chimney and a wavy brick wall, as well as a terracotta tile roof. Architect Jim Kellogg, a regular Wednesday walker and a former member of the Piedmont Planning Commission pointed out that the house also has a unique brick garage to the right, and that there is a swimming pool in the back. It was then time to retrace their steps and head back to the Exedra. It had been a 3-1/2 mile walk in a little more than 90 minutes with natural beauty that can only be enjoyed this time of year. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday, rain or shine, at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. The Housing Element is one of the seven state-mandated elements of the local General Plan and is required to be updated every eight years. The City of Piedmont is preparing the 2023- 2031 Housing Element Update to comply with the legal mandate that requires each local government to identify adequate sites for housing to meet the existing and projected housing needs for varying income-levels in the community. It is intended to provide the city with a comprehensive strategy for promoting the production of safe, decent and affordable housing, and affirmatively furthering fair housing during the housing cycle. The Housing Element Update establishes goals, policies, and actions to address the existing and projected housing needs in Piedmont. articles.text: Former Piedmont resident Mitchell W. Winters, a decorated veteran of the United States Marine Corps and a police officer in Arizona, committed suicide last November. This past Sunday, February 20, 2022, a warehouse full of dedicated fitness enthusiasts came together on a brisk holiday weekend morning to raise money in Mitch’s memory for The National Suicide Prevention Lifeline. The event, called the Winter Warrior workout and held in Phoenix, Arizona, was a rousing success. It raised more than $13,000 and more than 90 people participated. The Winter Warrior workout was the brainchild of James Stratman, the owner and founder of Modern Warrior and Peak Nutrition, which sell curated nutrition supplements to people trying to peak or perfect their physical fitness. First responders and veterans are often part of that community. James didn’t know Mitch and hadn’t even met him. But Mitch took physical fitness seriously, and word of his tragic and untimely death had circulated within that community. When James learned of Mitch’s story, he wanted to do something, through his companies, to help first responders and veterans. “Great companies do more than sell products or services,” James said. “Great companies give back in ways that help to bring about positive change. Awareness around and the damage from suicide in our veteran and first responder communities needs to change.” And thus was the Winter Warrior event born. Because James’ companies underwrote the cost of the event, 100% of its proceeds – every last nickel – will be donated to the Lifeline. The event itself was both fun and grueling. After they signed in and donated, the participants walked to a large open warehouse floor. On it were arranged a deceptively simple array of exercise equipment: attack bikes, boxes for stationary jumps, weights, jump ropes, and mats for burpees. Harmless enough just to look at, but quite taxing once they began to be used for the 20-minute workout. “That was a seriously tough workout. I was panting at the end,” said James, who is very disciplined about his own fitness. James and his team reached out to our family early on, to let us know what they were planning in Mitch’s memory. James said that he was hesitant about asking any of us to participate, because he suspected that we were still raw with grief about Mitch’s death. James was right about the grief still being very raw. But suicide in these communities is a silent and deadly epidemic. Police and firefighters are five times more likely than civilians to suffer from PTSD and depression. And the number of veteran and active duty suicides is more than four times the number of military operation deaths since 9/11. That is a ghastly statistic, and it needs to change. We are so grateful that James and his team reached out. On a personal level, this event was the first thing that has energized me since Mitch’s death. It was amazing that this group of strangers, whom Mitch had never even met, put in the hard work to prepare an event like this. James and his team are big thinkers, and this Winter Warrior event is just the first. James hopes to get ten times the number of participants and donors next year. The Winters family is joining forces with them and will be starting a charitable foundation, the Winter Warrior First Responders Foundation. Each year, it will raise money for the benefit of a family or individual who has been damaged by a first responder suicide or veteran suicide. As with this first Winter Warrior event, the plan is for 100% of the proceeds to go to that family or individual. Not the net proceeds– every last nickel. James and our family have big plans for this, and we’ll have more to report in the coming months. This first Winter Warrior workout was an extraordinary event. Mitch would have loved it. If the event had been in someone else’s memory, he would have happily and enthusiastically done the workout and then cheered others on.
